title: V3-5 — Thermal and Moisture Movement: Everything Breathes

concepts.title: Everything breathes — give it somewhere to go
concepts.mechanism: Concrete, block, and other materials expand and contract with temperature, and there is no way to simply stop that from happening. If you restrain a long run of concrete rigidly with no planned place to move, it doesn't just sit still — it builds up internal stress until it cracks, wherever the material happens to be weakest, which is rarely where you'd want. A control joint (a deliberate weak line sawn or formed into the concrete) doesn't prevent cracking — it decides WHERE the inevitable crack happens, in a place you planned for and can seal, instead of somewhere random and unsightly.
concepts.mechanismPro: Control joints go at planned intervals (spacing rules of thumb by slab thickness and exposure) sawn early enough to catch the shrinkage crack; expansion joints are a different, larger-movement detail for true dimensional change, not shrinkage. Climate determines which enemy dominates — heat-cycling here vs. freeze-thaw elsewhere.
concepts.hook: Perforated paper tears cleanly along the dotted line because that's the planned weak spot — tear it without the perforation and it rips wherever it wants. A control joint is the perforation you cut into concrete on purpose.

applied.prompt: A long exterior concrete walkway is being poured with no control joints, to save a small amount of sawcutting labor. Your call?

options.label: Require control joints at proper spacing before the pour proceeds
options.outcome: Right. The concrete WILL crack from thermal/shrinkage movement regardless — the only choice is whether that crack happens at a joint you planned and can seal, or randomly across the slab.

options.label: Allow it but require joints in the highest-visibility/highest-risk sections only
options.outcome: Reduces the worst-case appearance risk but leaves other sections to crack unplanned — a partial fix, not the full one.

options.label: Allow the pour without joints to save the labor cost
options.outcome: The walkway cracks anyway — you just don't get to choose where, and random cracks are harder to seal and worse to look at than planned ones.

applied.debrief: The same law also runs through V3-6's crack-reading: a thermal/shrinkage crack that shows up unplanned is exactly the kind of crack pattern that module teaches you to recognize as 'preventable, if you'd planned a joint.' Movement is not optional; where it happens is.

summary: Materials change size and you can't stop them — only plan for them. Restrain concrete's movement and it makes its own room: it cracks. Joints are you deciding where the cracks go. Wood moves with moisture, not heat. And climates differ in WHICH enemy dominates — the transferable literacy. PLAIN: give movement somewhere to happen. PRO: control vs expansion joints, sawcut windows, EMC and acclimatization, exposure classes.

sections.heading: Heat, restraint, and joints
sections.body: PLAIN: Heat things and they grow; cool them and they shrink. Concrete and steel grow about the same per degree — the happy accident that makes reinforced concrete possible. A 100-ft concrete face through a 50°F swing moves about a third of an inch — small, but concrete is so stiff that PREVENTING that movement takes enormous force, so unjointed concrete makes its own room: it cracks. Joints are the whole philosophy: you decide where the cracks go instead of letting the concrete decide. PRO: CTE ~5.5×10⁻⁶/°F concrete, ~6.5 steel; 'restraint cracking' (movement + something holding still = crack); CONTROL joints are deliberate weak lines — sawcuts in slabs (spacing in feet ≈ 2–3× thickness in inches: a 4-in slab gets joints every 8–12 ft; cut within the 4–12 hour window — after the slab holds a saw, before it cracks on its own schedule) — vs EXPANSION/ISOLATION joints, real gaps with flexible filler letting big pieces move independently: long bulkhead runs, building wings, slab-to-column isolation. And drying shrinkage needs no temperature at all: concrete shrinks ~0.05% as it dries over months — a 100-ft slab wants to lose ~5/8 in, the reason new slabs crack with zero temperature change. 'The joints are the design' is a sentence your structural engineer will respect.

sections.heading: Wood moves with moisture
sections.body: PLAIN: Wood barely notices temperature but swells and shrinks with humidity — much more across the grain than along it. Doors stick in the rainy season and rattle in March. You don't fight it: ACCLIMATIZE (let wood reach local moisture before installing), leave movement gaps, fasten so movement is allowed. In this climate exterior wood also stays damp enough to invite rot and termites — why Bahamian construction is a concrete culture with wood confined to ventilated roofs and finishes. PRO: equilibrium moisture content ~12–15% outdoors here vs 6–9% in conditioned interiors — wood moved from a humid warehouse into a chilled condo shrinks AFTER installation (the gapped-floor callback); 'acclimatize the material'; 'tangential vs radial shrinkage.'

sections.heading: The comparative lesson: which enemy dominates where
sections.body: PLAIN: In cold country the killer is FREEZE-THAW — water in concrete pores freezes and expands ~9%, a jack inside the stone cycling hundreds of times a winter, which is why northern concrete is air-entrained (microscopic bubbles giving ice room to push) and why the Bahamas skips air-entrainment entirely: you don't buy armor for an enemy that never comes. Hot-arid country fights giant daily swings (double the movement math) and flash-drying. Your tropical-marine enemy list is heat-that-never-relents, humidity, salt, UV, and biology. Same physics everywhere; a different term dominates — a CM who knows WHICH term dominates WHERE can work anywhere. PRO: 'exposure class' is the code's way of saying which enemy applies: F for freeze-thaw, C for corrosion/chlorides (yours), S for sulfates.

quiz.teach: Sawcut control joints must exist before the slab's own shrinkage stresses beat them to it.
quiz.prompt: The slab crew wants to sawcut joints 'tomorrow morning' after a late-afternoon pour. Why is timing the whole question?

choices.text: The window is roughly 4–12 hours: after the slab can hold a saw without raveling, but BEFORE it accumulates enough shrinkage stress to crack on its own schedule — tomorrow morning may be after the slab already chose its own crack lines
choices.why: Correct. A control joint that arrives after the random cracks is decoration. In this heat, the window leans early — night pours often get cut before dawn.

choices.text: Morning cutting is fine — concrete needs a day to be sawable
choices.why: Backwards on both ends: modern early-entry saws cut within hours, and hot-climate slabs build shrinkage stress fast. Waiting a day forfeits the race.

choices.text: Timing is aesthetic — cracks happen regardless
choices.why: Cracks happen regardless — WHERE is the decision. The joint invites the crack to a straight, sealed, maintainable line instead of a random wander.

choices.text: Joints should be cut before the pour
choices.why: That's tooled/formed jointing, an option for some work — SAWCUT joints by definition happen after placement, inside the window.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: cut the tidy line before the slab draws its own messy one — there's a window, and heat shrinks it. PRO: 'early-entry saw, 4–12 hours, spacing 2–3× thickness in feet; the joint layout is on the drawings, the timing is on the super.' (V3-5)

quiz.teach: Control joints and expansion joints solve different problems.
quiz.prompt: The 1,400-ft bulkhead cap needs joints. Which kind, and why is this worth a design-review hour?

choices.text: Both: control joints at regular spacing deciding where shrinkage cracks go, AND true expansion joints with flexible filler and waterstops at longer intervals letting the run move — 1,400 ft of restrained concrete in daily sun WILL move, and every unplanned crack is a chloride highway
choices.why: Correct. Long exposed marine runs need the full joint hierarchy — and in chloride service, joint design is corrosion design: cracks are ingress paths (S9).

choices.text: Neither — the cap is continuous for strength
choices.why: A 'continuous' 1,400-ft cap is continuous until its first summer, then it's jointed wherever it decided to crack — unsealed, over your rebar.

choices.text: Just pour it in short segments over several weeks
choices.why: Segmented pours create joints by default — cold joints, unplanned and undetailed. The design question (spacing, waterstops, sealant) still needed answering; you just answered it accidentally.

choices.text: One expansion joint in the middle
choices.why: 700 ft between movement provisions is ~350% over any sane spacing — the concrete will supplement your one joint with dozens of its own.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: a very long concrete ribbon in the sun needs planned places to crack AND real gaps to breathe. PRO: 'control joints at design spacing, expansion joints with waterstops at intervals, sealed — in the splash zone, joint discipline IS durability discipline.' (V3-5, S9)

quiz.teach: The vapor-barrier flip is the classic climate-literacy interview question.
quiz.prompt: A US-trained architect details the condo walls with an interior vapor barrier, copied from northern practice. What's wrong?

choices.text: Vapor drive here runs OUTSIDE-IN — hot humid exterior air pushing toward cool dry interiors — the exact reverse of cold climates; an interior barrier traps that moisture inside the wall against the cooled surface, farming mold in the assembly
choices.why: Correct. Barrier placement flips with climate: it belongs toward the warm-humid side. A Canadian wall detail in Nassau is a condensation trap with a permit.

choices.text: Nothing — vapor barriers are universal good practice
choices.why: The BARRIER is universal; its POSITION is climatic. Wrong-side placement is worse than none — it stops the wall drying inward, the only direction it had.

choices.text: Vapor barriers aren't needed in concrete construction
choices.why: Concrete moderates but doesn't exempt — interior finishes, furring, and insulation still create condensation planes that need managed vapor design.

choices.text: The problem is the material, not the position
choices.why: Any material in that position does the damage — the physics is WHERE the condensation plane lands relative to the barrier, not what the barrier is made of.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: moisture pushes from the hot wet side toward the cool dry side — here that's outside-in, so the wall must dry toward the room, not be sealed from it. PRO: 'vapor drive reverses in tropical climates; barrier toward the exterior side, assembly dries inward — the single best example of why climate literacy matters.' (V3-5, V3-9)

mathProblems.title: Thermal movement of a long element
mathProblems.context: Movement (inches) = length (ft) × 12 × CTE × ΔT. For a compact version: movement per 100 ft ≈ 0.0066 in per °F of swing at concrete's CTE. Multiply the swing by that rate.

decisionPoints.title: The imported hardwood deck
decisionPoints.scenario: The beach club's design calls for imported hardwood decking. The shipment arrives at 18% moisture content from a humid container, and the installer proposes laying it immediately into the shaded, breeze-cooled, partially air-conditioned beach club structure — 'hardwood is stable, that's why you paid for it.' The install window is tight against the opening date.

options.label: Stack and sticker the decking on site for acclimatization, measure MC until it approaches the service environment's equilibrium, then install with specified movement gaps
options.outcome: The wood sheds its container moisture BEFORE the fasteners lock it down — the shrinkage happens in the stack, not the deck. The opening date takes a modest hit that the punch list would have taken anyway, in gap form.

options.label: Install now — the schedule needs it and hardwood is stable
options.outcome: 'Stable' means slower, not immune: at 18% MC into a drier service environment, every board shrinks after installation — gapped decking, proud fasteners, cupped boards at the AC boundary. The callback is literal: wood moved from a humid warehouse into a chilled space shrinks in place.

options.label: Install now but spec kiln-dried-to-service-MC for future orders
options.outcome: Half a lesson: the future spec is right, and this shipment still shrinks in the deck. Fixing procurement going forward doesn't dry the boards going down this week.

decisionPoints.debrief: Wood equilibrates to its environment whether you schedule it or not — the only choice is whether the movement happens in the acclimatization stack or in the finished work. Measure MC, match it to service conditions, gap for the residual. (V3-5)
